title: "Price & Performance"
subtitle: "How engine power, body style, and brand prestige shape what you pay"
page-layout: full
toc: false
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(plotly)
library(scales)

msrp_df <- read_csv("data/processed/msrp_merged.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
n_total_msrp <- nrow(msrp_df)
n_mainstream <- sum(msrp_df$msrp <= 250000)
```

Does paying more for a car always buy you a stronger engine, or are buyers mostly paying for body style and badge prestige? Across nearly ten thousand vehicles, we look at how horsepower and sticker price move together—focusing on engine horsepower since public specification sources leave torque unrecorded.

## Horsepower vs. Price by Body Style

::: {.plot-container}
```{r}
#| label: fig-hp-msrp-faceted
#| echo: false

faceted_df <- msrp_df |>
  filter(msrp <= 250000) |>
  mutate(
    hover_text = paste0(
      "<b>", year, " ", make, " ", model, "</b><br>",
      "Style: ", body_style, "<br>",
      "Horsepower: ", comma(horsepower), " hp<br>",
      "MSRP: ", dollar(msrp)
    )
  )

p_body_scatter <- ggplot(
  faceted_df,
  aes(x = horsepower, y = msrp)
) +
  geom_point(aes(text = hover_text), color = "#d90429", alpha = 0.35, size = 1.3) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    se = FALSE,
    color = "#111111",
    linewidth = 0.75
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ body_group, ncol = 4) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(suffix = " hp")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_dollar(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k")) +
  labs(
    title = paste0(
      "Horsepower vs. MSRP Across Body Styles (N = ",
      comma(n_mainstream), " Vehicles)"
    ),
    x = "Horsepower",
    y = "MSRP ($ Thousands)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

ggplotly(p_body_scatter, tooltip = "text", height = 500) |>
  layout(
    autosize = TRUE,
    margin = list(t = 45, r = 20, b = 50, l = 60)
  ) |>
  config(responsive = TRUE)
```
:::

More horsepower pushes prices upward in every category, but two-door sporty cars climb much faster than everyday family or work vehicles. Coupes and convertibles shoot steeply into luxury territory as power rises, while pickups and minivans pack strong towing engines without the steep luxury markup. Economy hatchbacks stay clustered in the most affordable, lower-powered corner of the market. *(Ultra-rare hypercars above $250k are set aside here so everyday price trends stay easy to read.)*

## Best Horsepower Value by Brand

::: {.plot-container}
```{r}
#| label: fig-hp-per-dollar-mfr

mfr_summary <- msrp_df |>
  mutate(
    hp_per_1k = horsepower / (msrp / 1000),
    hp_per_dollar = horsepower / msrp
  ) |>
  summarize(
    n_models = n(),
    mean_hp_per_1k = mean(hp_per_1k),
    mean_hp_per_dollar = mean(hp_per_dollar),
    mean_hp = mean(horsepower),
    mean_msrp = mean(msrp),
    .by = make
  ) |>
  filter(n_models >= 30) |>
  mutate(
    make = fct_reorder(make, mean_hp_per_1k),
    tier = case_when(
      mean_msrp >= 100000 ~ "Exotic / Ultra-Luxury",
      mean_msrp >= 40000 ~ "Luxury",
      TRUE ~ "Mainstream"
    ),
    hover_text = paste0(
      "<b>", make, "</b> (n = ", comma(n_models), " vehicles)<br>",
      "Value: ", round(mean_hp_per_1k, 2), " hp per $1,000<br>",
      "Avg Power: ", round(mean_hp, 0), " hp<br>",
      "Avg MSRP: ", dollar(round(mean_msrp, 0))
    )
  )

n_mfr_vehicles <- sum(mfr_summary$n_models)

p_mfr <- ggplot(
  mfr_summary,
  aes(x = mean_hp_per_1k, y = make, fill = tier, text = hover_text)
) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(suffix = " hp/$1k")) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Mainstream" = "#d90429",
      "Luxury" = "#555555",
      "Exotic / Ultra-Luxury" = "#111111"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = paste0(
      "Horsepower per $1,000 Spent by Manufacturer (N = ",
      comma(n_mfr_vehicles), " Vehicles)"
    ),
    x = "Horsepower per $1,000 of MSRP",
    y = NULL,
    fill = "Segment"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

ggplotly(p_mfr, tooltip = "text", height = 620) |>
  layout(
    autosize = TRUE,
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = -0.09),
    margin = list(t = 45, r = 20, b = 65, l = 95)
  ) |>
  config(responsive = TRUE)
```
:::

Mainstream automakers deliver far more raw muscle per dollar than luxury or exotic badges. Everyday brands like Dodge, Kia, Chevrolet, Hyundai, and Ford sit right at the top because they offer strong engines at approachable prices, whereas European luxury and supercar makers sit near the bottom—showing that high-end buyers pay heavily for interior craftsmanship, handling, and prestige rather than cheap horsepower.

## Average Price by Body Style

::: {.plot-container}
```{r}
#| label: fig-avg-msrp-body

body_summary <- msrp_df |>
  summarize(
    n_vehicles = n(),
    mean_msrp = mean(msrp),
    median_msrp = median(msrp),
    mean_hp = mean(horsepower),
    .by = body_group
  ) |>
  mutate(
    body_group = fct_reorder(body_group, mean_msrp),
    hover_text = paste0(
      "<b>", body_group, "</b> (n = ", comma(n_vehicles), " vehicles)<br>",
      "Average MSRP: ", dollar(round(mean_msrp, 0)), "<br>",
      "Typical (Median) MSRP: ", dollar(round(median_msrp, 0)), "<br>",
      "Average Power: ", round(mean_hp, 0), " hp"
    )
  )

p_body_msrp <- ggplot(
  body_summary,
  aes(x = mean_msrp, y = body_group, text = hover_text)
) +
  geom_col(fill = "#111111", width = 0.65) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_dollar()) +
  labs(
    title = paste0(
      "Average MSRP Across Body Styles (N = ",
      comma(n_total_msrp), " Vehicles)"
    ),
    x = "Average MSRP",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

ggplotly(p_body_msrp, tooltip = "text", height = 390) |>
  layout(
    autosize = TRUE,
    margin = list(t = 45, r = 20, b = 45, l = 95)
  ) |>
  config(responsive = TRUE)
```
:::

Convertibles and coupes cost roughly twice as much on average as any other body style, largely because almost all exotic sports cars and grand tourers are built with two doors. Practical styles—including sedans, SUVs, pickups, wagons, minivans, and hatchbacks—stay much closer to mainstream family budgets, with hatchbacks serving as the most affordable entry point.

## A Note on Historical Prices vs. Newer Cars

Because public specification tables for recent 2022–2027 models do not publish sticker prices, the price charts on this page draw from verified 2001–2017 vehicle MSRPs while our other tabs explore newer 2022–2027 models directly. Since 2017, new-car prices and turbo/electric horsepower have both climbed noticeably, so these charts best capture how brands and body styles position themselves *relative* to one another rather than today's exact showroom sticker tags.
